prize_parts.citation: For the conception, construction and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments, which made possible the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson.

statement.case_for: The Higgs boson is the clearest case on the shortlist of nature supplying the decisive clue: a particle predicted in 1964 was found in 2012 by two independent detectors, completing the Standard Model. The 2013 prize honoured the theory, so the discovery is still unrecognised, and a decade of coupling and mass measurements has settled what was found. The chair asked for a principled rule. Mine is that the prize should go to the people whose conception and construction of the instruments made a discovery in enormous backgrounds possible, in both experiments, rather than to whoever held an elected spokesperson role on the day of the announcement. That rule is written into the citation, which names ATLAS and CMS, and it gives Jenni (ATLAS), Della Negra and Virdee (CMS). It does not remove the arbitrariness of three people standing for thousands, but it is a rule I can state and apply to every name.
statement.case_against: The case against is serious. A leadership prize is not the same as scientific authorship of the discovery, and Gianotti, whose role at the announcement is the most visible public link to the result, is left out. The configuration is also weighted two to one towards CMS. Five colleagues doubt that project leadership can ground a prize at all, and the Higgs may be read as an extension of 2013. B001 has far broader support (seven of eight members had it in their top three) and cleaner, more mature experimental credit. If the committee cannot accept a leadership-based citation, I would prefer B001 to a configuration I cannot defend.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001 with an experimental trio (Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger) and doubts that leadership can be rewarded in place of specific scientific contribution.
responses.response: I accept part of the objection and have changed my configuration because of it: I drop Gianotti, because a spokesperson role at announcement is the weakest form of the leadership claim, and I move to the conception and construction leaders. For a detector-driven discovery the instrument is the scientific contribution, and it is a contribution that can be dated and documented, which a collaboration role at one moment cannot. Where I disagree is on maturity and breadth. B001 is excellent, but Mehlig himself notes that analogue simulation has mostly reproduced known physics so far. The Higgs result settled an open question about nature. I keep B001 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, proposes Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee for B020 as founding leaders of ATLAS and CMS and discloses an instrumentalist bias.
responses.response: I now arrive at your trio, but by a different route and not for the reason of consensus. In round 1 I preferred Gianotti for her visibility at the announcement. The chair's question forced me to state a rule, and visibility is not a rule I can defend in a citation. Because you disclosed an instrumentalist bias, I checked my reasoning separately: it rests on the discovery being unrecognised and mature, not on a preference for hardware. I still think the choice among four names cannot be settled from the file alone, and I would not oppose Gianotti if the committee prefers to weight the announcement.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B011 to B001 and proposes Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, a mixed theory and experiment prize, with Cirac and Zoller not to be rewarded twice.
responses.response: Mixing Zoller into an experimental prize answers my earlier worry that theory alone is a weak fit, and it handles the overlap with B011 well. I find the combined citation more coherent than the experimental-only version. My hesitation is that the third name then excludes Esslinger and Cirac, and Jaksch is not on the list, so the theory credit is incomplete however it is cut. That is the same three-person problem I have with B020. On that ground I do not rank the two cases apart; I rank B020 higher because its open question about attribution is smaller than its scientific clarity.

responses.point: Eriksson and Olsson prefer B041, arguing that the flat-band discovery is robust whatever the pairing mechanism and that the citation can be built around the discovery.
responses.response: That is a fair statement of the case and I think the answer to the chair's question is partly yes: the discovery of correlated states at the magic angle is robust. My reservation remains the omission of Cao and Dean, which Eriksson and Olsson both concede, together with a field about eight years old. Waiting costs little here, while the Higgs has been waiting since 2012. I would support B041 in a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the Higgs discovery as distinct from the 2013 prize, which I judge it is but cannot settle from the file.
Whether project leadership of two detectors is an adequate basis for a prize, and whether three names can fairly represent two collaborations; the choice of Virdee over Gianotti is a close call.
Whether the committee would prefer the broadly supported and mature B001 to a harder attribution on B020.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict identified for any shortlisted entry. I know of no personal or institutional connection to Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee, Gianotti or any other credited person, and my own work in string theory and cosmology is not in competition with any of the candidates.
